lead: Supercharging forces more air mass into the same swept volume. More trapped air allows more fuel, so a smaller engine can give the power of a larger one. The blower is driven from the crankshaft, so it costs engine power; the useful figure is the net gain. Superchargers appear in performance petrol cars, aircraft at altitude, and some industrial diesels. This chapter covers the objectives, the main mechanical types, the density ratio, and the effects on knock, thermal load and exhaust. Exhaust-driven boosting follows in 4.6.
prereq: You need: swept volume and volumetric efficiency from Unit 1, and knock from Unit 3; charge cooling is in 4.7.

blocks.text: A naturally aspirated engine fills the cylinder with air near ambient pressure, about 1.0 bar. Its torque is limited by the air mass trapped each cycle. A supercharger raises the intake pressure above ambient; the ratio p₂/p₁ is the pressure ratio, using absolute pressures. The mass trapped also depends on temperature: hot air is less dense. For a perfect gas, density ratio is pressure ratio times the inverse temperature ratio. A boost to 1.6 bar sounds like 60 percent more air. If compression heats the air from 300 K to 340 K, the density ratio is only (1.6/1.0) × (300/340) = 1.41, so about 41 percent more air.

blocks.where: ρ is density in kg/m³; p is absolute pressure; T is absolute temperature in K; subscript 1 is ambient before the blower, subscript 2 is after the blower.

items: More power for the same swept volume and better power-to-weight ratio.
Altitude compensation: a blower restores sea-level air density when ambient pressure falls.
Sometimes lower specific fuel consumption, because friction and engine weight are spread over more kW.

blocks.text: All mechanical superchargers are driven by a belt or gears from the crankshaft. The roots blower has two meshing lobes that trap a fixed volume of air and push it to the intake. It is a positive-displacement machine: flow per revolution is nearly constant, so boost rises with engine speed. The sliding-vane blower uses vanes in a rotor to trap and move air; it is simple but the vanes wear. The centrifugal blower uses a fast impeller to throw air outward; pressure rises roughly with tip speed squared. It is efficient at high speed but gives little boost at low speed.

Positive-displacement blowers give strong low-speed response. Centrifugal blowers suit high-speed power. The figure shows the air path through a belt-driven supercharger; the pressure rises, but temperature also rises.

sections.h3: Drive power and the net gain

blocks.text: The blower takes power from the crank. The honest output is net brake power: P_net = P_gross − P_drive, where P_gross is the power from the extra trapped air and P_drive is the compressor work plus belt and gear losses. P_drive often reaches 10 to 20 percent of gross power at high boost. This limits boost: drive power grows with mass flow and pressure ratio, and compression also heats the charge. The necessity is clear: more power density, altitude compensation and a smaller package. The limitations are also clear: the net gain is always smaller than the density ratio suggests, and knock and thermal load grow.

items: Peak cylinder pressure and temperature rise, so pistons, valves, head gasket and bearings face higher thermal and mechanical load. Cooling and lubrication must be upgraded.
In SI engines, boost raises end-gas pressure and temperature, so knock tendency rises. Common fixes are a lower compression ratio, higher-octane fuel, retarded spark and charge cooling; see 4.7.
In CI engines, more air mass reduces smoke at a given fuel rate, but higher temperature can raise NOx; injection timing may need adjustment.
Exhaust mass flow and exhaust temperature rise. The exhaust manifold must withstand thermal cycling, and back pressure must stay low enough for good scavenging.

Modifications for supercharging include lower compression ratio, stronger pistons and gasket, larger cooling and oil capacity, fuel enrichment and intercooling. A blower is not a simple bolt-on for a standard engine.
Emissions change: more power per litre, but higher NOx is possible; after-treatment and calibration must match the boost.

spec.title: Mechanical supercharger path
spec.aria: Air passes from a filter at 1.0 bar and 300 K through a belt-driven supercharger into the intake manifold at 1.6 bar and 340 K, then into the engine.

examples.question: A 1.5 litre petrol engine gives 75 kW naturally aspirated with intake air at 1.0 bar and 300 K. A belt-driven supercharger raises the intake manifold to 1.6 bar absolute and 340 K. The blower absorbs 11 kW from the crank at this speed. Find the density ratio, the gross power if power follows trapped air mass, the net power, and the percentage gain over the naturally aspirated engine.
steps: Use absolute pressures and temperatures: p₁ = 1.0 bar, T₁ = 300 K, p₂ = 1.6 bar, T₂ = 340 K.
Net power = gross power − blower drive power = 105.88 − 11 = 94.88 kW.
examples.answer: Density ratio 1.41; gross power 105.88 kW; net power 94.88 kW; gain 19.88 kW, about 26.51 percent.
examples.check:
p1 = 1.0
T1 = 300.0
p2 = 1.6
T2 = 340.0
P_na = 75.0
P_drive = 11.0
dr = (p2 / p1) * (T1 / T2)
gross = P_na * dr
net = gross - P_drive
gain = net - P_na
pct = gain / P_na * 100.0
print(f"{dr:.2f}")
print(f"{gross:.2f}")
print(f"{P_drive:.2f}")
print(f"{net:.2f}")
print(f"{gain:.2f}")
print(f"{pct:.2f}")

traps: Using gauge pressure in the pressure ratio. p₂ and p₁ must be absolute; a gauge reading of 0.6 bar is 1.6 bar absolute if ambient is 1.0 bar.
Forgetting charge heating. 1.6 bar at 340 K is not 60 percent extra mass; the density ratio is 1.41.
Quoting gross power. The belt-driven blower takes crank power, so the exam answer is net power.
Assuming supercharging always lowers specific fuel consumption. It can, but at high boost the drive loss, fuel enrichment and knock control can worsen it.
Mixing knock effects. Boost raises knock tendency in SI engines, so compression ratio is lowered or fuel octane raised; it is not increased.

quiz.q: Define supercharging and state one objective.
quiz.a: Supercharging is raising the intake air density above ambient by a crank-driven blower. One objective is more power from the same swept volume.

quiz.q: Why is the density ratio smaller than the pressure ratio?
quiz.a: Compression heats the air. Density falls as temperature rises, so the temperature ratio divides the pressure ratio: ρ₂/ρ₁ = (p₂/p₁)(T₁/T₂).
Roots blower, sliding-vane blower and centrifugal blower.

quiz.q: A 2.0 litre engine gives 100 kW at 1.0 bar and 300 K. A supercharger raises intake air to 1.5 bar and 320 K and absorbs 8 kW. Find the density ratio, gross power and net power.
Why is a crank-driven supercharger limited to moderate boost?
quiz.a: Drive power rises with mass flow and pressure ratio and comes from the same crank. Compression heating lowers the density gain and raises knock and thermal load, so high boost gives diminishing net gain.

quiz.q: State two effects of supercharging on SI engine knock and how they are controlled.
quiz.a: Boost raises end-gas pressure and temperature, so knock tendency rises. Control by lowering compression ratio, cooling the charge, retarding spark or using higher-octane fuel.

quiz.q: A driver says a 1.6 bar boost gives 60 percent more power. Correct this statement using temperature and drive power.
quiz.a: The density ratio includes heating: (1.6/1.0)(300/340) = 1.41, so trapped air rises about 41 percent, not 60 percent. The blower also takes crank power, so net gain is lower still.

beyond: Not for the exam. Production superchargers today are often roots-type blowers on petrol engines, while centrifugal units appear in aftermarket kits and some aircraft engines. Engineers choose positive displacement for low-speed response and centrifugal for high-speed efficiency. The next search terms are compressor map, positive displacement versus dynamic compressor, and roots blower efficiency. Thermal management and emissions push designs toward intercooling and hybrid assistance for the blower drive.
